title: Building Reading Skills Through Phonological Awareness
source_title: Marshall E-News | Smore Newsletters for Education

blocks.content:
READING 

CORNER READING CORNER

Title Talk  Reading Corner November Newsletter Literacy Focus: Phonological Awareness, Phonemic Awareness and PhonicsBuilding Strong Foundations for ReadingPhonological and phonemic awareness are important early literacy skills that help children develop the foundation they need to become successful readers and writers.What is phonological awareness?Phonological awareness is the ability to hear and work with the sounds in spoken language. Children develop this skill by recognizing rhyming words, clapping out syllables, identifying words that begin or end with the same sound, and playing with sounds in words.What is phonemic awareness?Phonemic awareness is a specific part of phonological awareness. It focuses on identifying, hearing, and manipulating individual sounds, called phonemes, in spoken words. For example, children may identify the first sound in the word sun, blend the sounds /c/ /a/ /t/ to say cat, or change a sound to make a new word. These skills help children connect spoken sounds to letters and build the skills needed for reading and spelling.What is Phonics?Phonics is the relationship between letters and the sounds they represent. Children learn to connect written letters and letter combinations with sounds to help them read and spell words.For example, children learn that the letter B represents the /b/ sound, as in ball, and that the letters sh represent the /sh/ sound, as in ship.Fun Activities Phonemic Awareness Activities to Try at HomeRhyming Time: Say a word, such as cat, and ask your child to think of words that rhyme with it, such as hat, bat, or mat.Clap the Syllables: Clap the parts of family members’ names or everyday words. For example, ap-ple has two syllables, while ba-na-na has three.Sound Detectives: Choose a letter sound and ask your child to find objects around the house that begin with that sound.Beginning Sound Game: Ask your child what sound they hear at the beginning of words such as moon, dog, or fish.Blend the Sounds: Say individual sounds slowly, such as /m/ /a/ /p/, and encourage your child to put them together to say map.Change a Sound: Ask your child to change the first sound in cat from /c/ to /b/. What new word did they make? (Bat!)Fun Phonics ActivitiesLetter of the Day: Choose a letter and practice its sound. Find objects around the house that begin with that sound.Sound It Out: Help your child say each sound in a simple word, such as /c/ /a/ /t/, and blend the sounds together to read cat.Letter Match: Match uppercase and lowercase letters and practice saying their sounds.Build a Word: Use magnetic letters or letter cards to build simple words like sun, dog, and map.Read Together: While reading a book, point out familiar letters and words. Encourage your child to identify letters and connect them to their sounds.Note: Phonological awareness focuses on hearing and playing with sounds in spoken language, while phonics connects those sounds to written letters. Both skills help children develop strong reading and spelling foundations!Remember: Learning about sounds should be fun! Just a few minutes of playful sound activities each day can help children strengthen their early literacy skills and build confidence as they begin their reading journey.

summary: November's literacy focus explains **phonological awareness, phonemic awareness, and phonics**—essential building blocks for reading and writing success. **Phonological awareness** involves hearing and working with sounds in spoken language (rhyming, syllables), **phonemic awareness** focuses on individual sounds (phonemes) in words, and **phonics** connects written letters to sounds. The newsletter includes fun at-home activities like rhyming games, sound detective hunts, syllable clapping, and word-building exercises to help children develop these skills through playful practice.

title: K-5 Grading System Changes for 2026-2027
source_title: Marshall E-News | Smore Newsletters for Education

blocks.content:
DISTRICT 

INFORMATION DISTRICT INFORMATION

Changes to the K-5 Grading System at Talawanda NEW for the 2026-2027 School Year Grades 3-5 - Moving to a Traditional Letter Grading System (A-F)We are excited to shift our grades 3–5 to a traditional letter grade system (A-F) to provide a more detailed look at your child's overall performance and academic habits. This change aligns our 3rd-5th graders with the expectations they will meet in middle and high school, fostering greater accountability and preparing them for future success.For families, this transition offers a familiar and intuitive way to track progress. While the numerical scale focused on specific milestones, letter grades allow for a wider range of feedback to distinguish between meeting basic requirements and consistently exceeding them. This system ensures a clearer dialogue between teachers and parents, highlighting exactly where a student excels or may need extra support.Here is the breakdown of the traditional letter grading system:A - 90-100%B - 80-89%C - 70-79%D - 60-69%F - 0-59%Grades K-2 - Remaining with the Numerical Grading System (1-4)Grades K–2 will continue using the numerical (1–4) grading system to best support our youngest learners. At this foundational level, education is focused on the progressive development of core skills and meeting specific developmental milestones rather than a cumulative letter grade. The 1–4 scale provides a precise way for teachers to communicate exactly where a student is in their learning journey—from beginning to explore a concept to achieving mastery—ensuring that families have a clear understanding of their child's growth in these critical early years.As a reminder, here is a breakdown of the numerical scores:4 - Consistently/Independently Meeting the Standard3 - Meeting the Standard2 - Approaching the Standard1- Not Yet Meeting the Standard

summary:
**New grading systems effective for the 2026-2027 school year:**
- **Grades 3-5**: Transitioning to traditional **letter grades (A-F)** to align with middle/high school expectations and provide clearer feedback on performance (A: 90-100%, B: 80-89%, C: 70-79%, D: 60-69%, F: 0-59%)
- **Grades K-2**: Continuing with the **numerical system (1-4)** to track developmental milestones (4: Consistently/Independently Meeting Standard, 3: Meeting Standard, 2: Approaching Standard, 1: Not Yet Meeting Standard)

source_title: Marshall E-News | Smore Newsletters for Education

blocks.content:
VOLUNTEER 

& 

VISITOR 

POLICY VOLUNTEER & VISITOR POLICY

As we continue with our volunteer policy this year, please remember that any adult volunteer who wishes to enter the school building must have a volunteer application on file with the office every school year. After a parent’s second visit to the building, they are required to complete fingerprinting and a background check through the Central Registration Office. Please plan to complete this process at least 3 weeks prior to the event. This allows adequate time for the background check to be completed and for the appropriate information to be provided to the school administrator for planning purposes. Once completed, your background check is valid for 5 years.Central Registration Office:Ruth Michael📞 513-273-3101We appreciate your understanding and cooperation as we work to keep our students, staff, and school community safe. Public schools have implemented these regulations to comply with state and federal safety requirements regarding volunteers and visitors in schools.

summary: All adult volunteers must have a volunteer application on file each school year. After a second visit, volunteers must complete **fingerprinting and background check** through the Central Registration Office at least **3 weeks prior** to events. Background checks are valid for 5 years. Contact Ruth Michael at **513-273-3101** for Central Registration.

title: Class at the Court Field Trip
source_title: Marshall E-News | Smore Newsletters for Education

blocks.content:
IMPORTANT 

UPDATES 

& 

REMINDERS IMPORTANT UPDATES & REMINDERS

2026 Class @ the Court Greater Oxford Educational CollaborativeMiami University Athletics & Talawanda Elementary SchoolsOn Wednesday, November 11, 2026 our students once again have the fantastic opportunity to attend the Miami University Women’s basketball game “Class at the Court” at Millett Hall during the school day. Thanks to the generous support of Miami University and our educational partnership our students will attend the game free of charge.We will leave school shortly after we take attendance, heading to Millett Hall at 9:30AM, and will return to school after the game. Any student that has NOT arrived at school on 11/11/26 before 9:30AM, will not be able to participate in this activity. Please make note of this. We will contact the parent of any student that experiences illness or behavior issues and the parent will need to pick their student up at Millett Hall. Permission slips will be shared with our families the last week in October.

summary: **Talawanda Elementary Schools** students will attend a **Miami University Women's Basketball game** at **Millett Hall** on **Wednesday, November 11, 2026**. Students must arrive at school before **9:30 AM** to participate; buses depart at 9:30 AM after attendance. The event is **free** thanks to Miami University partnership. **Permission slips** will be distributed the last week of October.
